courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Memory cost, ablations, failure modes and gsplat in practice
md: 3DGS trades memory for speed: hundreds of megabytes of explicit parameters instead of a few megabytes of network weights, in exchange for rendering at well over 30 FPS and training in tens of minutes.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Add-one-in vs leave-one-out on a fixed harness
md: Removing a stage is not always a clean subtraction. You must decide what replaces it: no rewrite at all, or a trivial rewrite; BM25 alone, or BM25 with more candidates to keep the reranker's input size equal. State the replacement, because different choices give different deltas.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: SWE-bench: how one patch gets graded
md: Resolved means: the patch applies, and **every** FAIL_TO_PASS test and **every** PASS_TO_PASS test is found and passes. Fixing the issue while breaking one old test scores exactly the same as doing nothing.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Designing tools: the agent-computer interface
md: Treat tool design like UI design for a new colleague: clear names, documented parameters, concise high-signal output, guardrails that turn likely mistakes into instructive errors. Changing the tool often beats changing the prompt.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Why an agent saying done is not evidence of done
md: Verification turns "the agent says it is done" into "independent evidence says it is done". How much you can trust a shipped result is bounded by how often the verifier passes wrong results.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Reward design: hidden tests, partial credit and judges
md: Partial credit is not automatically better. A reward that counts tests which already passed pays the agent for the starting state, so on hard tasks the policy can learn that touching nothing beats trying. Credit only the change you want, and make breaking existing behavior cost something.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Why AI text needs a planted signal
md: The hard rule damages **low-entropy** text, where one continuation is nearly forced. The paper's example: "Barack" is almost always followed by "Obama", yet "Obama" may be on the red list. Code and memorized text have the same problem. The next lesson fixes this with a soft bias.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: What an allocation trace records and why you would replay it
md: Live bytes are not RSS. RSS counts whole pages the process has touched, including allocator metadata, rounding and free holes. The gap between the two is the overhead you are usually hunting.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Local Outlier Factor: density compared with your neighbors
md: scikit-learn's LocalOutlierFactor has two modes. With novelty=False (the default) only fit_predict and negative_outlier_factor_ exist. With novelty=True you get predict, decision_function and score_samples, but the docs warn to call them only on new data: scoring the training points that way gives wrong results, and predict will not match fit_predict.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Commit, abort with CLRs, and fuzzy checkpoints
md: A checkpoint is not a point where the disk is consistent. A fuzzy checkpoint only records which transactions were active and which pages were dirty. Redo usually has to start **before** the checkpoint, at the smallest recLSN in the DPT, because a page dirtied long ago may still be unflushed.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Input-type bugs in real pipelines
md: Record the model id and the input type (or exact prefix string) alongside the index, and check them at query time. When either changes, build a new index and switch over, rather than re-embedding part of the old one in place.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Why waiting on threads is expensive and coroutines are cheap
md: Async does not make one request faster. It makes **waiting cheap**: a waiting connection costs a small saved object instead of a blocked OS thread with its own stack, so a few threads can serve many thousands of mostly idle connections.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Compare-and-swap: write only if nothing changed, else retry
md: CAS compares values, not history. If the value goes from A to B and back to A between your load and your CAS, the CAS succeeds as if nothing happened. For a counter that is harmless. For pointers in lock-free data structures it can be a real bug, the **ABA problem**, which has its own course later.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Why research needs a loop, not one retrieval
md: A research agent is not a bigger retrieval call. It is a harness loop whose next query depends on what the last read revealed, and whose output is a set of claims each tied to a source.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: On-demand capacity: tokens per minute and the max_tokens trap
md: Set `max_tokens` close to the longest answer you really need. The AWS docs say it directly: if you hit TPM quotas earlier than expected, reduce max_tokens to better approximate your completions. Measure real output lengths from the `OutputTokenCount` metric.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Running ternary models fast: I2_S, lookup tables, real numbers
md: bitnet.cpp's kernels are **lossless**: they reproduce the training-time quantization exactly. On 1,000 prompts with a 700M BitNet b1.58 model, I2_S, TL1 and TL2 matched an FP32 reference token for token 100% of the time, versus 1.4% for llama.cpp's TQ1_0 and TQ2_0, which quantize activations in 256-element blocks unlike training.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Branchless code: cmov, masks and lookup tables
md: Branchless code trades a *possible* misprediction for *always* doing the work of both sides plus the select. Always check the compiler output (Compiler Explorer, `-S`) before hand-rewriting: the optimizer may already have done it, or may have a good reason not to.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Choosing an engine: tradeoffs, write stalls and failure modes
md: Misconception: "LSM-trees have no write amplification because they only write sequentially." They write sequentially, but every byte is rewritten as it moves down levels: about 33x in RocksDB's leveled example. The win is in I/O pattern and batching, not in writing less, and on some workloads a B+tree writes fewer bytes.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Why drop the tokenizer, and why raw bytes are expensive
md: Bytes remove the vocabulary and its blind spots, but multiply the number of positions by roughly 4. Since compute is about $2mT$, a byte model is only practical if the big network runs on far fewer positions than there are bytes.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Why C memory bugs compile cleanly and ship
md: C's type system cannot express *who owns this block* or *how long this pointer is valid*. Rust's ownership and borrow rules are exactly that missing information, checked at compile time.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Cache lines: the cache moves 64 bytes, never just one
md: A common misconception is that memory cost is proportional to the bytes your code reads. It is proportional to the **lines it touches**. Reading 8 bytes from each of 1,000 scattered lines moves 64,000 bytes through the hierarchy.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: The local replacement model makes every edge linear
md: Matching the real model's outputs exactly on prompt $p$ does not mean the local replacement model uses the same mechanism. The paper compares it to a Taylor approximation: it agrees at the point and drifts as you move away, which is why interventions are needed later.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Small propensities, high variance, and clipping
md: Clipping changes what the estimator measures. A clipped rank is systematically undervalued, which pushes documents shown low back down, the same direction as the original position bias. Tune $\tau$ on held-out data and report it.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: What k-means actually optimises
md: Inertia is the *entire* definition of a good clustering in k-means. Anything you believe about your clusters that inertia does not measure, such as "this point is an outlier" or "this group is a long thin chain", k-means cannot express.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Arrow in memory: buffers, validity bitmaps and offsets
md: A column in memory is a few flat buffers: values (or offsets plus data) and a validity bitmap. Flat, typed, contiguous buffers are what make tight loops and SIMD over columns possible.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inlining: removing a call unlocks every other optimization
md: Inlining matters less for the call it removes than for what it enables: constant folding, dead code removal and vectorization inside the merged body. It costs code size, and it only works when the callee's body is visible in the same compilation.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: The observe-act loop: screenshots in, mouse and keyboard out
md: Misconception: the model "sees" the screen continuously. It sees only the screenshots you return, at the moments you return them. If a dialog pops up after your capture, the model does not know about it until the next screenshot.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: How loom takes over the scheduler and walks every schedule
md: Every source of non-determinism must come from loom: no real time, randomness or I/O inside `loom::model`. Determinism is what lets loom replay a schedule and flip one choice at a time.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: iCT, sCM, LCM and the other few-step distillers
md: Failure modes and costs: distillation (CD, LCM, PD) is capped by the teacher's quality. Adversarial losses (ADD) bring GAN training complexity. The sCM paper notes that variational score distillation methods such as DMD can produce overly smooth samples with limited diversity. Continuous-time CM training was unstable until sCM's fixes. And 1-step quality still trails the multi-step teacher.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Why hash mod N reshuffles almost every key
md: The goal of consistent hashing: when the set of servers changes, move only the keys that must move, which is about $K/N$ keys for $K$ keys and $N$ servers, and never shuffle keys between servers that did not change.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Elasticsearch bool: filter context versus query context
md: A `should` clause is not an OR filter when the query also has a `filter` or `must` clause, because minimum_should_match then defaults to 0. Putting a hard requirement in `should` silently turns it into a mere preference. Set `minimum_should_match` explicitly if you need at least one of several options to match.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: SAT solvers: DPLL, unit propagation and clause learning
md: CDCL = DPLL + conflict analysis that learns a clause + backjumping to the level that clause asserts + watched literals for cheap propagation + activity-based decisions and restarts. Each conflict teaches the solver something it never has to rediscover.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: A five-turn session: diffs, state and generated queries
md: Strict mode guarantees the diff is **schema-valid**, not that it is **right**. A perfectly typed `{"remove": []}` for *drop the salary limit* is still a wrong state. Schema enforcement removes parsing failures; only evaluation (lesson 6) catches meaning failures.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Plausible is not faithful: the biasing-feature test
md: Faithfulness is a causal claim about what drove the answer. You test it by intervening, not by reading. A biasing feature that flips answers without ever being mentioned proves the CoT omitted a real cause.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: A worked pipeline: four chunks, and the copy-bound crossover
md: Overlap hides the smaller stages behind the largest one; it never removes the largest one. Your speedup ceiling is $(\sum_s t_s) / (\max_s t_s)$, reached as $n$ grows, and in the steady state the pipeline runs at the rate of its slowest stage. Before adding streams, work out which stage that is. If it is already the kernel, overlap buys you the copies and nothing more.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Serving it: latency for 100 candidates and distillation
md: Reranker latency is about k divided by throughput. You control it with three knobs: how many candidates you rerank, how large the model is, and how many pairs you can run in parallel. Each trades against accuracy or cost.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Hopper mainloops: TMA, stages and warp specialization
md: A Hopper CUTLASS mainloop is a ring of shared memory stages: a producer warp keeps TMA loads ahead, consumer warpgroups run wgmma on full stages, and full and empty barriers pass ownership of each stage back and forth.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Worked example: what a CXL access costs
md: Treat CXL memory as a far NUMA node: same instructions, same caching, about 70 to 100 ns more per miss for a nearby device, bandwidth comparable to a DDR channel per x8 link. Whether it is a win depends on how many misses you send there.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Curation inside a domain: quality filters from phi-1 to FineWeb-Edu
md: A quality classifier encodes someone's definition of quality. If that definition was tuned by watching a benchmark, the filtered data can look great on that benchmark and lose breadth elsewhere. DoReMi's appeal is the opposite stance: it uses no downstream data at all. phi-1's authors also had to analyze possible HumanEval contamination in their data.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Choosing a layout: hot/cold splits, ECS chunks and columnar data
md: A common misconception, called out by Fabian himself: data-oriented design is not only about cache misses or splitting hot and cold fields. It is about designing around the data and the transforms on it. Layout is the most visible tool, not the whole method.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Replaying failures, the limits of DST, and who uses it
md: A passing simulation is only as good as its fault model and its oracles. If your simulated disk never loses unsynced writes, you have not tested crash recovery; if no oracle checks liveness, a stuck cluster passes.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why parallel decoding breaks, and how to make it fast
md: Do not read 'parallel generation' as 'all tokens in one step'. Quality drops quickly when many interdependent tokens are committed together; useful systems unmask a few to a few dozen tokens per pass depending on confidence.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Chunked prefill or disaggregation: when each one wins
md: Chunked prefill bounds interference inside one GPU; disaggregation removes it and lets each phase get its own hardware, parallelism and scale. Pick by measuring per-GPU goodput under your SLOs, prompt lengths and interconnect, not by architecture preference.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: The DPO loss on one preference pair, with real numbers
md: The weight $\sigma(\hat r_l - \hat r_w)$ is what makes DPO work. The authors report that a naive version without this weighting (push chosen up, rejected down, equally on every pair) can make the language model degenerate.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: How dual writes silently diverge, and how to contain it
md: Two independent writes have no shared order and no shared atomicity. Either keep one store authoritative and repair the other, or derive the second store from the first store's commit log.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Why run your tracing logic inside the kernel
md: The verifier is a **safety** check, not a security review. It proves your program cannot crash or hang the kernel; it does not judge what the program observes. That is why loading tracing programs requires root, or both the CAP_BPF and CAP_PERFMON capabilities.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Fewer operations and fewer weights, then shipping it
md: Order of operations for edge models: pick an efficient architecture and distill into it, quantize to int8 with per-channel weights, fall back to QAT if accuracy drops, prune only when your runtime benefits, and verify accuracy, latency and peak RAM on the actual device.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Budget forcing, effort levels and hard caps at inference
md: Inference-time levers are cheap but blunt: forcing a stop interrupts reasoning, forcing 'Wait' saturates. Training-time methods (preference pairs, length rewards, LCPO) teach the model to plan a shorter trace, which is why L1 beats budget forcing at small budgets.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Why raw strings break filters and joins
md: Normalize to an ID, filter on the ID, and keep the raw string for display and debugging. Run the **same** normalizer on queries and on profiles, or the two sides drift apart and matches silently disappear.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
md: **Readiness notification**: you give the kernel a set of file descriptors and it tells you which ones can do I/O right now without blocking. You still perform the `read` or `write` yourself. An **event loop** is a thread that repeatedly waits for readiness, then runs a short handler (a *callback*) for each ready descriptor.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: The winner's curse: why the best public score is too high
md: Misconception: "we never trained on the test queries, so the number is clean." Choosing among variants by their test score is training with a very small model: one decision per comparison. A hundred prompt tweaks checked against the same 50 queries is a hundred-way fit.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Four independent counters that refuse to scale
md: The unit of sharing between cores is the cache line, not the variable. Two variables in one line are shared as far as the hardware is concerned, whatever the source code says.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: FedAvg exactly, worked on three clients over two rounds
md: With $E = 1$, full batches and full participation, FedAvg is exactly full-batch gradient descent on the pooled objective. Everything interesting about federated optimization, good and bad, comes from doing more than one local step.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-1: expand at search time instead of build time
md: ACORN-$\gamma$ and ACORN-1 run the same search strategy, predicate subgraph traversal. They differ only in *where* the denser neighborhood comes from: stored at build time (ACORN-$\gamma$, faster search, slower build) or reconstructed from two-hop lookups at query time (ACORN-1, cheap build, somewhat slower search).

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Counting the work: FLOPs, bytes, and the exponential unit
md: Misconception: "attention is two GEMMs, so it runs at GEMM speed." The softmax between them is cheap in FLOPs but runs on units hundreds of times slower than the tensor cores. FP8 makes it worse: matmul throughput doubles while exponential throughput stays the same.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Generating data by following a velocity field from noise
md: A flow model is a learned velocity field plus an ODE solver. Flow matching makes the *training* of that field as cheap as regression; the *sampling* cost is the number of solver steps.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Ghost permissions, trusted bases and choosing a tool
md: Verification moves trust from "we tested enough" to "the spec says the right thing". Spend your review effort on the spec: the invariants, the environment actions you modeled, and every assumption or trusted function.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Why write() returning does not mean your data is safe
md: Calling fsync on a file does not necessarily make the file's **directory entry** durable. A newly created or renamed file also needs an fsync on a file descriptor for the directory, or after a crash the name may be missing.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Transpositions and Indel: which edits count changes the answer
md: Two libraries that both say "Damerau-Levenshtein" can disagree, and "ratio" in RapidFuzz is Indel based, not Levenshtein based. When a threshold copied from one tool behaves oddly in another, check which distance and which normalization each uses.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step
md: Quad code = coordinates of C and D in the frame where A is (0,0) and B is (1,1). Four numbers, independent of where the quad is, how it is turned, or how big it looks.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Better cells on the sphere: S2 cubes and H3 hexagons
md: H3 parent containment is only approximate. Seven hexagons cannot exactly tile a larger hexagon, so a child cell's area can stick out of its parent's boundary. The index hierarchy is exact logically (truncating an ID always gives the same parent), so aggregating by parent ID is consistent, but do not treat a parent's polygon as the exact union of its children.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Rounding, the small and large pools, and segment sizes
md: Every request is rounded to 512 bytes, routed by size (at most 1 MiB small, otherwise large), and served from a block in that pool. Only a miss touches the driver, with a 2 MiB, 20 MiB or rounded-to-2-MiB segment.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: From registers to HBM: the GPU memory map
md: Speed and capacity trade off at every level: registers and shared memory are on the SM and fast but small, L2 is shared by all SMs, and HBM is large but far away. Kernel design is mostly about making each byte fetched from HBM count.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Timeline first: where the 14.52 ms actually goes
md: The GPU utilization that Nsight Systems reports is **time** utilization, not resource utilization. Its own guide says so: a single running memcpy counts as the same amount of utilization as a huge kernel that takes over all the cores, and concurrent operations in the same chunk can add up to more than 100 percent. A 100 percent busy GPU can still be doing almost nothing useful.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: One kernel, many threads: grids, blocks and SMs
md: Blocks must not depend on each other. A thread may not wait for, or read results produced by, a thread in a different block of the same grid, because that block may not have been scheduled yet. (Thread block clusters, in lesson 4, are the one opt-in exception.)

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: From chunks to an entity graph with LLM extraction
md: The graph is an LLM's *abstractive summary* of the corpus, not a parse of it. Every node and edge carries an LLM-written description, and those descriptions, not the raw text, are what later stages summarize.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: RLVR: replacing the reward model with a program
md: Verifiable does not mean perfect. A verifier can reject correct answers (12.0 versus 12) or accept wrong ones (a unit-test suite that misses edge cases). Real pipelines normalize answers, for example Tulu 3 used the 'flex' MATH evaluation logic, and the quality of the checker caps the quality of the signal.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Service days, calendar exceptions and times past 24:00
md: A trip runs on date D if its service_id is active on service day D. Its times are offsets from noon minus 12 hours on D, may exceed 24:00:00, and are in agency_timezone. Anything you compute from the schedule must keep the pair (trip_id, service date), not just trip_id.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf record: sampling on overflow, and the skid problem
md: Without precise sampling, the "hot" instruction in `perf annotate` is often the one *after* the slow one, such as the instruction that consumes a load's result. Use `:pp` when you care about individual instructions.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Choosing, verifying and debugging huge pages in production
md: Do not over-learn the Redis story as "THP copy-on-write always copies 2 MiB". In current `mm/huge_memory.c`, a write to a shared anonymous THP splits the mapping and copies one 4 KiB page. What remains true is that fork-heavy writers churn their huge mappings, and the projects' own guidance (Redis: disable THP; PostgreSQL: THP currently discouraged, explicit huge_pages recommended) is what to follow.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Why BM25 and dense retrieval miss different documents
md: BM25 and dense retrieval fail on different documents. BM25 misses paraphrases; dense retrieval blurs exact identifiers, codes and rare names. Fusing the lists recovers documents either one would miss and promotes documents both agree on.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Solving for a homography with the DLT, by hand
md: A homography maps points only after dividing by the third coordinate. Code that multiplies by H and keeps the first two entries silently computes the wrong point everywhere except where W happens to be 1.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Submitting, waiting and how the kernel runs a request
md: Completions can arrive in **any order**. The ring preserves the order in which requests are *attempted*, not the order in which they *finish*. Always identify a CQE by its `user_data` (often a pointer to your per-request state), never by its position.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: tcmalloc: rseq per-CPU caches, spans and Temeraire
md: A restartable sequence must tolerate running its prefix many times, so everything before the commit must be side-effect free or harmless to repeat. Writing slot 5 twice is harmless here only because nothing reads beyond `current`.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Elle: catching isolation anomalies in transactions
md: Elle is sound but not complete. A cycle found is real, yet missing cycles prove nothing: appends never observed by a later read leave gaps in the version order, and predicate anomalies (like phantoms over WHERE clauses) are outside its analysis.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The per-packet budget: why the kernel path runs out of cycles
md: Misconception: bypass is mainly about avoiding copies. The kernel already offers zero-copy paths. At 14.88 Mpps the killers are fixed per-packet costs (interrupts, mode switches, metadata setup, shared locks), which is why minimum-size packets are the benchmark that matters.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Counting bytes: the chain before and after fusion
md: Fused bytes = what you must read + what you must keep. Everything in between is the saving. For a chain of k unary elementwise ops on the same tensor with no side outputs, eager moves about k times the fused bytes.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Distilling language models: tokens, sequences, on-policy
md: For language models, decide two things: what sequences you train on (references, teacher outputs, or the student's own samples) and which divergence you minimize (forward KL covers all modes, reverse KL picks one). On-policy training fixes the train-inference mismatch.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Quantizing keys per channel and values per token (KIVI)
md: Bits per number are not the whole cost. Group metadata adds bits (about 1 per number for FP16 scale and zero per 32), and the full-precision residual matters for short sequences.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Why the GPU prefix cache runs out, and where KV can go
md: Each tier down is roughly 10x bigger and slower. Offloading turns a prefix-cache miss into a load from a lower tier, which pays off only if the load is faster than recomputing.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Why wall clocks cannot order events across machines
md: A smaller wall-clock reading does not mean an event happened before another, and an event that did happen first can carry a larger wall-clock reading, as the last-write-wins example shows. Treat wall time as a hint, never as proof of order.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: MaxSim: each query token finds its best document token
md: Why max and not average? The ColBERT ablation replaced max with average similarity and MRR@10 dropped noticeably. In the toy, the *founded* row of Doc A averages (0.03 + 0.02 + 0.18 + 0.98 + 0.49) / 5 = 0.34, even though the document contains a near-perfect match. Averaging punishes documents for having other content.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: The continuous thought: hidden state in, hidden state out
md: n continuous thoughts cost n sequential forward passes at inference and n + 1 sequential passes per training example, with no tokens emitted for the latent steps.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: The last mile and the Recursive Model Index
md: An RMI separates model size from execution cost. A lookup evaluates exactly one model per stage, however many leaf models exist. Adding leaves makes each leaf's slice smaller and its error bounds tighter without adding work per lookup.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: From MLM logits to one weight per vocabulary term
md: Misconception: the expansion terms are synonyms. They are whatever the MLM head plus ranking training found useful. The paper's own example document about bow legs gains *leg* and *treatment*, but also *arrow* (bow and arrow) and *teeth*, with small weights.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaMART: boosted trees that fit the lambdas
md: LambdaMART = gradient boosted regression trees whose regression targets are the LambdaRank lambdas, recomputed after re-sorting at every round.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Why relevance labels are the bottleneck of search evaluation
md: An LLM judge does not remove the need for humans. Both Bing and the TREC studies check the judge against human labels, and Bing re-labels a stratified weekly sample with trained assessors to catch drift. Without a gold set you cannot tell whether the judge is right.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: LLM judges for generation: modes, biases and fixes
md: A safe default for generation judging: pairwise or rubric grading with the explanation before the verdict; both orders, with disagreement treated as a tie; report and control length; a judge outside the model families being compared; and a human-labelled subset to measure agreement before every major change.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Inside an inference server: one engine step at a time
md: The scheduler decides **what** runs each step, the KV cache manager decides whether it **fits**, and the executor just runs a forward pass over token ids and block tables. Almost every serving optimization in this course is a change to the first two.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: When the pool runs dry: admission control and preemption
md: Admission control is a bet about future output lengths. Reserve the worst case and you never preempt but waste memory; allocate on demand and you fit far more requests but need a preemption policy (latest arrival first, all of its blocks) and a recovery method (swap or recompute).

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Why hard constraints need filters, not similarity
md: The LLM never touches the documents. It only translates the query into a filter object. Exact enforcement is done by the search engine, which is cheap, deterministic and testable.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Calls and tokens per query for each method
md: Calls set the latency floor and the per-call overhead; tokens set the bill. Listwise minimizes calls, not tokens. PRP buys robustness to prompt order with 20 to 100 times more prompts than pointwise (220 to 1,100 times more than listwise) at k = 100.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pointwise: yes/no relevance and query likelihood
md: Both pointwise methods need token log-probabilities. Many chat APIs only return generated text, which is why the RankGPT authors could not run them on GPT-4. And because each passage is scored alone, the score must be comparable across passages (calibrated), which the PRP paper argues LLMs are not trained to provide.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: SIFT: keypoints across scale and a 128-number descriptor
md: A SIFT keypoint carries position, scale and orientation. The descriptor is computed in that local frame, which is why it survives zoom and rotation, and its 128 entries are L2-normalized and clipped for lighting robustness.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Why a preempted lock holder stalls everyone
md: Lock-free means a stalled thread can never stop the others: some operation always completes. It does not promise that any particular thread finishes, and it does not promise speed under contention.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Why one regular expression per format does not scale
md: A common dodge: "I will write regexes only for the formats I care about and drop the rest." You cannot know in advance which format you will care about during the next incident, and the lines you dropped are exactly the rare error templates. Dropping them also silently biases every count you compute afterwards.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Why models break past their trained length
md: Each RoPE pair has a wavelength $\lambda_d = 2\pi b^{2d/|D|}$. Pairs with $\lambda_d \ll L$ are safe at any length; pairs with $\lambda_d > L$ are the ones that break when you go past the trained window.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Does the model use its context? Evaluation
md: Do not trust a single number. Low perplexity, a passing passkey test and a large advertised window can all coexist with poor use of mid-context information. Test retrieval at many depths, multi-hop and aggregation tasks, and short-context regressions.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: When looping helps, when it hurts, and the design space
md: Looping buys **depth** (multi-step reasoning, using context), not **capacity** (memorized facts). Judge a looped model on reasoning tasks at matched FLOPs, not only on perplexity at matched parameters.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA
md: SISA is a training-time design decision. It cannot be retrofitted onto a model that was already trained on all the data, which is the situation for every existing LLM. That is why the rest of this course is about **approximate** unlearning: editing an existing model so it behaves *as if* it had been retrained, without a guarantee.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Why vector size is a cost knob, and why chopping a vector fails
md: Matryoshka training puts the most useful information in the first coordinates, so a prefix of the vector is a good small embedding. Without it, keeping the first m numbers of a normal embedding throws away information almost at random.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Pipeline parallelism: bubbles, 1F1B and the interleaved schedule
md: Bubble = (p - 1) / (v m). 1F1B bounds activation memory to p microbatches; interleaving divides the bubble by v at the cost of v times more pipeline sends.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Placement policy: where a block goes decides what survives
md: Separate policy from mechanism. Good policies (address-ordered first fit, best fit, segregated fit approximating best fit) gave near-zero fragmentation on real traces once implementation overheads were removed. The remaining job is to implement such a policy fast, which is what size-classed allocators do.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Acquire and release: publishing data across threads
md: Synchronization needs a pair on the same atomic: a Release (or stronger) write and an Acquire (or stronger) read that observes that write or its release sequence. Then everything before the write is visible after the read.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: RCU: publish a new version, free the old after a grace period
md: RCU protects readers from updaters, not updaters from each other. `rcu_assign_pointer()` does not make two concurrent updates safe; the example still takes `foo_mutex`. And a pointer from `rcu_dereference()` is valid only inside the critical section that fetched it.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Batch hard: mining the hardest pairs inside a P x K batch
md: Batch hard needs K of at least 2, or there is no positive to take a max over. And because it always picks the extreme pair, label noise and outlier crops dominate the loss: Hermans and colleagues show such outliers in Market-1501 and MARS in their supplementary material.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Noise, repetitions and when a difference is real
md: Misconception: "overlapping intervals prove the versions are equal". They show you could not detect a difference at this noise level. A smaller real difference may exist; to find it, reduce noise or take more runs.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: MoE routing replay and low-precision RL
md: "BF16 train, FP8 serve" is the lowest-friction mode, but it is not a contract: the docs say there is precision drift between the two paths, and on MoE workloads you should pair it with R3 and optionally TIS.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: LRB: learning to evict like a relaxed Belady
md: The **good decision ratio** (good evictions divided by all evictions) grades each eviction individually. The LRB authors found it correlates strongly with the final byte miss ratio, so they used it to choose features, model, loss and sizes from one simulation pass instead of hours-long full simulations per design.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: MLA in production: kernels, prefill, parallelism, results
md: MLA moves the cost of attention from memory to compute: one 576-wide row per token per layer, read by every head. That is a big win for decode, where memory traffic dominates, as long as you keep many heads on the GPU that holds the cache and use the non-absorbed form when compute dominates.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: The multi-query pipeline: generate, retrieve in parallel, merge
md: LangChain's synchronous `invoke` searches the generated queries **one after another** in a for loop; only the async `ainvoke` path runs them concurrently with `asyncio.gather`. LlamaIndex runs them concurrently when `use_async=True` (its default). If your multi-query latency grows linearly with N, check which path you are on.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Latency budgets and phased ranking in real engines
md: Defaults are shallow. Both Elasticsearch's rescore window_size and text_similarity_reranker's rank_window_size default to 10, so an unconfigured reranker can only shuffle the first page. Also keep the window fixed across pages: the docs warn that changing window_size while paginating can make top hits shift.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why a weight matrix is not a bag of independent numbers
md: Treat a weight matrix as a linear map, not a list of numbers. Its gradient has directions with very different strengths, and these optimizers rebalance those directions instead of rebalancing individual entries.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Why the best learning rate drifts as models get wider
md: muTransfer has three steps: parametrize the target in muP, tune a smaller version of it, copy the tuned HPs to the target. It works because muP makes the optimal HPs converge to fixed values as width grows.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: From a racy flag to a correct spin lock
md: Atomic does not mean cheap. An atomic write to a line that other cores are reading forces cache-line transfers, and in Bos's measurement it made another core's plain loads about 10 times slower on an older x86-64 machine.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Why a database keeps old copies of rows
md: MVCC trades space for concurrency: every update leaves an old version behind so that readers already in flight can keep a consistent view without blocking writers.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Paying for versions: VACUUM, HOT updates and XID wraparound
md: MVCC moves the cost of concurrency into the storage engine: dead versions to clean, index entries to maintain, and XIDs to freeze. Long-lived snapshots make all three worse.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Three branches: compress, select, and slide
md: The gates are independent sigmoids, not a softmax. They do not have to sum to 1, so the model can turn several branches up or down at once. Also note what NSA does *not* do: it keeps the full KV cache (and three branches with independent keys and values), so it cuts the bytes *read* per step, not the bytes *stored*.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: PDQ, learned copy detectors and building a real pipeline
md: Choose by the edits you must survive. Resizes, recompression and tone changes: a perceptual hash with Hamming search is cheap and exact. Crops, overlays, rotations and composites: a learned copy descriptor with nearest neighbor search. Either way, tune the threshold on labeled pairs from your own traffic.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: First touch: the thread that writes a page first picks its node
md: Reading is not touching. The `mbind(2)` man page notes that a first *read* of an anonymous page maps a shared page of zeros held by the kernel; no page is allocated on your node until the first *write*. A warm-up loop that only reads does not place anything.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Garbage collection and the write amplification formula
md: A drive does not know which LBAs your file system considers free. Unless told (lesson 4), every LBA ever written counts as live. Agrawal et al. put it bluntly: unlike a log-structured file system, the disk here is always full, so cleaning pressure is maximal all the time.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Scoring a detector: precision, recall, AP and COCO mAP
md: AP measures ranking quality across all thresholds for one class; COCO mAP averages it over 10 IoU thresholds and all classes. When comparing papers, check which one is reported: AP50 and AP@[.5:.95] differ a lot for the same model.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Tiered storage versus S3-native: choosing a design
md: Tiered storage moves *old* data to S3 and leaves the write path alone. S3-native moves the *write path itself* to S3, trading commit latency for stateless compute. Hybrids like Neon put a small quorum log in front so commits stay fast while object storage holds the bulk.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: SLOs, error budgets, burn-rate alerts, and the 03:00 dashboard
md: Alert on symptoms, not causes. The SRE book's advice is to focus much more effort on catching symptoms than causes, and to worry about a cause only when it is very definite and very imminent. A page saying "cache hit rate dropped" is a cause; a page saying "users are burning the checkout budget at 20x" is a symptom, and it stays correct when the cause next time is something else.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Adding layout: from LayoutLM boxes to OCR-free Donut
md: Layout-aware models add *where* to *what*: each word's box becomes embedding lookups, so a model can learn that a value sits right of its key. OCR-free models fold reading into the network and emit structure directly.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: CUDA builds: PTX, cubins and the architecture list
md: Cubins run only on the same major CC with an equal or higher minor; PTX JIT compiles forward to any equal or higher CC. Ship cubins for the GPUs you target plus PTX for the newest one, and keep the list short for development builds, because every entry multiplies CUDA compile time.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Diagnosing and fixing flaky tests: order, state and timing
md: Flaky means uncontrolled state. Reproduce with the exact node id, order seed and loop count, find the state, and control it with a fixture. Reruns and quarantine are temporary and cost real signal.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Review by email: patch versions and trailer tags
md: Whatever the tool, the author's loop is the same: answer every comment, change the code where the reviewer was right, record what changed between versions, and carry earned review credit forward only while it still applies.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Fork, clone and two remotes: origin and upstream
md: Misconception: "syncing my fork" updates my laptop. GitHub's Sync fork button updates the fork on GitHub; `git fetch upstream` plus a merge updates your local copy. GitHub's docs point out that syncing locally does not update the fork on GitHub until you push. They are separate repositories.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Sign-off, the DCO, and how your commits land upstream
md: Misconception: `-s` signs the commit. It does not. `-s` (lowercase) adds a Signed-off-by text trailer, a legal statement. `-S` (uppercase, `--gpg-sign`) adds a cryptographic signature that GitHub can show as Verified. A project may require either, both, or neither.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Inbound licensing: inbound=outbound and contributor agreements
md: Outbound is what users get; inbound is what the project gets from you. Inbound=outbound needs no paperwork; a CLA is a one-time signed grant, often with an explicit patent license and a statement about your employer.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Reporting honestly: geomeans, many benchmarks and costs
md: Do not cherry-pick. Quoting only the best benchmark, dropping a regressed one, or rerunning until a borderline result flips are all ways to make noise look like a win. Reviewers who rerun your commands will find out.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: What a maintainer needs: a failure they can run themselves
md: A screenshot of a traceback is not complete. The maintainer cannot search it, copy the line numbers, or paste it into a test. Stack Overflow's guide says plainly: do not use images of code; paste text.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Why a reviewer sends a big pull request back
md: The right size for a PR is **one self-contained change**: it does one thing, includes its tests, and leaves the system working. Line counts are a symptom; focus is the goal.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Why contiguous KV allocation wastes most of the memory
md: Decoding is memory-bound, so throughput comes from batch size, and batch size comes from how many KV caches fit. Any slot that is reserved, fragmented, or duplicated is a request you could not batch.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, and when caching pays
md: Prefix caching never changes outputs. It reuses KV for exactly the same tokens instead of recomputing it, so its effects are on speed and memory (outputs can differ only by the tiny floating-point noise any change in batching causes). It helps exactly as much as prefill dominates the work and prefixes repeat.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: A profiling workflow, its costs and its blind spots
md: Comparing two flame graphs by eye is error-prone because widths are relative to each graph's own total. To check a fix, record both under the same load and diff the folded files (a differential flame graph), and make sure you have enough samples for the change to stand out from noise.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: How the compiler lays out a struct, field by field
md: Two rules give every struct layout: **each field's offset is a multiple of its alignment**, and **the struct's size is a multiple of its own alignment** (the largest field alignment). Everything else, including all the padding, follows from these.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Real-time tracking, 3D lifting and joint angles for apps
md: Keypoints are noisy, especially when occluded. Before writing rules on them: check per-keypoint visibility or score, prefer 3D world landmarks or a side view for sagittal angles such as the knee, smooth over a few frames, and use two thresholds (hysteresis) rather than one.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Latency versus bandwidth: two different walls
md: **The one thing to remember:** ask whether the next address is known before the current load finishes. If not, you are latency-bound and more bandwidth will not help. If yes, you are probably bandwidth-bound and the question becomes how many bytes you move.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: How a PRM is trained and how it scores a solution
md: A PRM is a per-step classifier read off in one forward pass. Training labels stop at the first error. To compare solutions you reduce step scores to one number; product and minimum perform similarly, but product quietly favours shorter solutions.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: What a switch really costs: direct work and cold caches
md: Misconception: "a context switch costs a few microseconds, so it does not matter." That is the direct cost on an idle cache. Li et al. found the total ranged from several microseconds to more than a thousand, depending on working set size and access pattern. Benchmarks that touch no data hide the part that hurts.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned prompts are brittle
md: Prompt optimization is search: candidates (instructions and demos), a metric, a dev set to score on, and a proposer. Everything else in this course is a choice of proposer, a way to spend the budget, or a way to keep the final number honest.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Sequence design, then the self-consistency check
md: Self-consistency grades a generator with a predictor that was trained on natural proteins, and both can be wrong in the same direction. A design that AF2 loves is not proven to fold: it has passed one cheap filter. Everything after this point costs money and weeks.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Conversational rewriting: turning a follow-up into a standalone query
md: Misconception: the rewriter should make the query richer. Its job is to make it *standalone and faithful*. A rewriter that adds guessed facts (say, `when the leader fails during a network partition`) can steer retrieval toward documents the user never asked about. Instruct it not to answer, and to return the message unchanged when it is already standalone.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Computing the estimate with popcount, and re-ranking by the bound
md: Per vector, the query-time work is a few AND plus popcount passes over the D-bit code and a handful of multiply-adds with precomputed factors. The error bound then tells you which candidates are worth an exact distance.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Indexing: how chunk size and overlap decide what can be found
md: Small chunks lose their context. D1.5 reads *or adoption. Send leave requests to the People team, who approve them.* It never says which leave. In a real handbook with ten leave policies it would match every leave question equally well. Bigger chunks keep context but dilute the embedding and spend more of the prompt.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Document, query and interaction signals: freshness, popularity, clicks
md: Shape raw signals before the model sees them: turn age into a decaying freshness, counts into logs or rates, and remember that query-only features can only matter through interactions.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? Paired tests, effect sizes, many systems
md: Compare systems on per-query differences, with a paired t-test or randomization test, and report the mean difference with a confidence interval and effect size. With many systems, control the familywise error instead of running dozens of independent tests.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: WebSocket: one HTTP upgrade, then a two-way framed stream
md: Masking is **not encryption**: the key travels in the same frame. RFC 6455 requires it (even over TLS) so that a script in the browser cannot choose the exact bytes on the wire. Without it, an attacker could craft upgraded traffic that a broken proxy reads as an HTTP request and caches, the cache-poisoning attack in section 10.3. Use `wss://` (TLS) for confidentiality.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: From a sparse rating matrix to item-to-item recommendations
md: Treating a blank as a rating of 0 is a modelling choice, not a fact. It makes plain cosine reward items that are merely *rated by the same people*, whatever the ratings. In Sarwar et al.'s MovieLens experiments, adjusted cosine gave lower error (MAE) than plain cosine or Pearson correlation.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Evaluating recommenders without fooling yourself
md: Split by time, exclude what the user already consumed, beat tuned simple baselines, and confirm with an online experiment.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Aggregation and sorting: running state, hash tables and spills
md: A GROUP BY result from a HashAggregate has no defined order. If you need sorted output, write ORDER BY; do not rely on the order you happened to see.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When a high score stops meaning a solved task
md: Misconception: reward hacking means the RL algorithm is buggy. DeepMind's analysis points the other way: the behavior comes from misspecification, and a *better* optimizer is more likely to find an intricate loophole that a weaker one would miss. Stronger RL makes the specification matter more, not less.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: One RL step is five workloads on two kinds of engine
md: A common misconception is that a bigger training cluster speeds up RL roughly linearly. Training is often a minority of the step. If generation is two-thirds of the time, even infinitely fast training saves at most a third.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Measuring achieved bandwidth with a copy kernel
md:
Common traps:
- **Arrays that fit in L2.** An 8 MB array on an H100 (50 MB L2) measures cache bandwidth, not HBM.
- **Mixing GB and GiB.** 2,982.6 GB/s is 2,777.8 GiB/s. Use one divisor for both theory and measurement.
- **Timing the first launch** or using host timers without synchronizing.
- **Uncoalesced or strided access**, which measures your access pattern, not the memory.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Why fuse ranks instead of scores
md: RRF needs only positions. Scores on different scales, scores that drift between index versions, even systems that expose no scores at all can be fused, because $1/(k + r)$ is the same function of rank for every input.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Bindings, helpers, abstractions: the layers under a Rust driver
md: Unsafe code is concentrated in reviewed subsystem abstractions. A driver written only against those abstractions cannot cause undefined behavior, *provided the abstractions are sound* and every `unsafe` block honours its contract. That proviso is the whole game; lesson 6 shows what happens when it fails.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
md: Inserting a task into a local DSQ is a commitment. Once there, it waits for that CPU even if another CPU goes idle a microsecond later. Schedulers that want work sharing keep tasks in a shared custom DSQ and move them to a local DSQ only when a CPU asks via `ops.dispatch()`.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill
md: A common misconception: self-play means no external signal. Games have a perfect, free judge: the rules decide who won. Take that away and a model playing against itself only amplifies its own beliefs, which is the collapse setting from the prerequisite course.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: What is safe to cache: scoping, context and invalidation
md: Never let the cache cross users for answers that depend on who is asking: balances, orders, permissions, anything personal. A false hit there is not a quality bug; it is a data leak. Scope by user or tenant, or bypass the cache for those requests entirely.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Cache-aware scheduling: queue order sets the hit rate
md: Scheduling cannot create reuse; it can only avoid destroying it. The DFS bound (sum of tree edges) is the floor on prefill work, and ordering decides whether a tight cache reaches it.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
md: A CH query must not stop the first time the two searches meet. The meeting node with the best sum may be found later. Each side stops only when its own queue minimum is at least the best sum found so far.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: One instruction, many lanes: SIMD registers and lane counts
md: A SIMD register is a small array of lanes. One instruction does the same operation on every lane. Lane count = register width / element width, so 4, 8 or 16 floats for 128, 256 or 512 bits. Vertical (lane-wise) work is cheap; horizontal (across-lane) work costs shuffles.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Shipping SIMD: -march levels, runtime dispatch, portability
md: Compile for what you can require, dispatch for what you cannot. -march levels give the compiler AVX2 or AVX-512 everywhere but crash on older CPUs; target_clones, __builtin_cpu_supports or is_x86_feature_detected! pick the best version per machine at run time.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Three modules, one loop: how slime is laid out
md: The Data Buffer is not a separate server process you deploy. It is the data source object that the rollout side uses to fetch prompts and to hold returned groups (for example partially generated samples). With the default object-store transport it is `RolloutDataSourceWithBuffer` (straw transport uses `QueueDataSource`), and `--data-source-path` replaces it.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Why single neurons are hard to read: superposition
md: Superposition: a layer with $d$ dimensions can represent many more than $d$ sparse features as almost-orthogonal directions, at the cost of interference. Neurons then mix many features, so we look for directions instead.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features
md: High variance explained is not full understanding. Sonnet's SAEs explained at least 65% of variance, so a sizeable part of the activation lives in the error term, and a latent's top activating examples do not prove what it does. Use ablation or steering to check.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in map coordinates
md: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in 2D or 3D coordinates. Simple kriging is the zero-mean GP on residuals; ordinary kriging adds an unknown constant mean; universal kriging adds trend basis functions; the nugget is observation noise.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Drafting without a second model: Medusa heads and token trees
md: Not every tree method is lossless. Medusa's optional **typical acceptance** keeps a candidate if the target's probability exceeds $\min(\epsilon, \delta e^{-H(p)})$, a threshold that depends on the entropy $H$. It raises speed at higher temperatures but no longer samples from the target's distribution. Medusa-2 also changes the backbone weights, so outputs differ from the original model.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Long audio, streaming and hallucinations in production
md: Long-form and streaming ASR are decoding problems layered on a fixed-window model: the window moves by predicted timestamps, unstable text waits for agreement, and silence must be removed or detected before the decoder invents something to say.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: TLB reach, huge pages and shootdowns
md: TLB reach = entries x page size. Working sets beyond it pay a page walk on most random accesses; huge pages raise reach by 512 times, and every unmap in a multithreaded process may interrupt other CPUs.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Two clocks: why sensor readings arrive out of order
md: Misconception: "out of order is rare, so I can ignore it". In the toy, 5 of 12 readings arrive after a reading with a later event time. Mobile, battery-powered and intermittently connected devices make this the normal case, not an edge case.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Why recurrence was the bottleneck for sequence models
md: The Transformer's core bet: replace the recurrent chain with attention, so every position can read every other position in one layer and the whole layer runs as parallel matrix multiplications.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Training recipe, quadratic cost and what changed since 2017
md: Attention trades sequential steps for quadratic pairwise work. That is a great deal on GPUs for moderate n, and the reason long-context methods all target the n x n score matrix.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Next-token prediction: turning raw text into training examples
md: `block_size` is the **maximum** context, not the only context. Because position $t$ in each chunk sees only $t+1$ tokens, the model is trained on every context length from 1 to `block_size`, which is exactly what it needs when generation starts from a short prompt.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: A derivative is the slope you see when you zoom in
md: The derivative is not the change in $f$ over a big step. It is a rate at one point. For $x^2$ at 3, a step of $+2$ actually raises $f$ by 16, not $6 \times 2 = 12$, because the slope itself changes along the way. This is exactly why gradient descent takes small steps.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backpropagation: the chain rule run backward through a graph
md: Gradient checks can fail for honest reasons: at a kink such as ReLU at 0 or a max with ties, the function is not differentiable and the two sides disagree. Check at random points away from kinks, and in double precision.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
md: Status 0 means success; 128 + N means killed by signal N. Start scripts with `set -euo pipefail`, quote every expansion, send errors to fd 2, and exit non-zero on failure so the next tool in the chain can tell.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Math-bound or memory-bound: arithmetic intensity and the roofline
md: Intensity counts HBM traffic, not every load. Good kernels tile data into shared memory and registers so each HBM byte is reused many times; a naive kernel that re-reads HBM has a much lower effective intensity than the formula suggests.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: From hello.c to a running process
md: Misconception: "the compiler makes something the CPU runs straight off the disk." The CPU only fetches instructions from memory. An executable is inert until the OS loader maps it into a process's memory and points the CPU at its entry point.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: every process gets its own addresses
md: Every address your program uses is virtual. The MMU translates it on every access using the current process's page table, the TLB makes that fast, and page faults let the OS fill in memory lazily.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Reward over-optimization, best-of-N and modern recipes
md: A higher reward model score is not evidence of a better model. Teams track KL and check with fresh human or held-out evaluations, because the proxy keeps climbing after real quality has turned down. This is Goodhart's law applied to learned rewards; the Reward hacking course goes deeper.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Ranking with vectors and cosine similarity
md: The vector space model scores a document by the cosine between its tf-idf vector and the query's. Engines compute it by streaming the query terms' postings into accumulators, so documents that share no query term cost nothing.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and strings
md: A pointer does not know how many elements it points to. Whoever passes a buffer must also pass its length (or rely on a terminator such as the zero byte), and every write must be checked against that length.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Moves, Copy and clone: why let s2 = s1 kills s1
md: Assigning, passing, or returning a non-`Copy` value moves it. To keep using the original, either `clone()` it (pay for a copy) or lend it out with a reference (next lesson).

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The dot product: one number that measures alignment
md: A dot product of 0 does not mean the vectors are unrelated in every sense; it means they are **perpendicular** (orthogonal). And a big dot product does not by itself mean similar direction: it can come from long vectors. When you want direction only, normalize first or use cosine.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Loss: turning "fits the data" into one number
md: A loss turns "fit the data" into one number that depends on the parameters. Squared error is the negative log-likelihood under Gaussian noise; cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood for class probabilities. Training means minimizing it.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Why a single linear layer cannot learn XOR
md: A hidden layer only adds power because of the nonlinearity between layers. Without it, any stack of layers is one linear map in disguise.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: CPU scheduling: turnaround time versus response time
md: No policy wins on every metric. SJF and STCF minimize average turnaround but give long waits before a job first runs; round robin gives fast response but stretches every job's completion. Choosing a scheduler means choosing which metric you care about.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayes' rule: why a 90 percent accurate test is often wrong
md: The classic mistake is confusing $P(E \mid H)$ with $P(H \mid E)$, called base rate neglect. It shows up in ML as a classifier with high recall on a rare class still producing mostly false alarms. Precision is $P(\text{positive class} \mid \text{flagged})$ and depends on the base rate; recall is $P(\text{flagged} \mid \text{positive class})$ and does not.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Why loss falls on a straight line in log-log space
md: A scaling law turns each multiplicative step in scale into a fixed **ratio** of loss. Fit the exponent on cheap runs, then extrapolate. Small exponents (around 0.05 to 0.1 here) mean big scale-ups buy modest gains.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Why you need a test collection before you can say better
md: trec_eval ignores the rank column of a run file. It sorts by the score column and breaks ties by document id, so a run whose scores disagree with its ranks gets evaluated in score order, not the order you intended.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Why keyword match misses meaning and cross-encoders are too slow
md: Misconception: *semantic search understands meaning*. It finds vectors that are geometrically close, and closeness means whatever the training pairs rewarded. A model trained on question-answer pairs puts a question near its answer, not necessarily near a paraphrase of the question.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
md: The product of training is an **ordered list of merges**. Order matters: rank 1 is the first merge learned. The vocabulary is just the alphabet plus every merge result, and the next lesson shows that encoding new text replays this list in order.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Learning rate: the stability limit, warmup, decay and clipping
md: Clipping must go **after** `loss.backward()` and **before** `optimizer.step()`. Karpathy's list of silent bugs includes clipping the *loss* instead of the gradients, which simply ignores outlier examples instead of taming their updates.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Tuning ef and M, and choosing between HNSW, IVF and PQ
md: Filtered vector search is the most common production surprise. Post-filtering an ANN result can return fewer than k rows and silently lower recall. Check whether your engine pre-filters, post-filters or scans iteratively. hnswlib, for example, accepts a filter in knn_query that restricts results to allowed ids.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What happens when your program calls write
md: Two traps in the convention. The 4th argument goes in `r10`, not `rcx` as in a normal C call, because the `syscall` instruction itself overwrites `rcx` with the return address. And after the call, `rcx` and `r11` are garbage from your point of view. Compilers know this; hand-written inline assembly must list them as clobbered.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Why the average hides the requests users remember
md: Report latency as a distribution: several percentiles (p50, p99, p99.9) plus the maximum, not a mean. The mean blends a few terrible requests into many good ones and describes no actual user.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Normalizing partial dates and Present against a reference date
md: *Present* and a missing end date are not the same thing. *Present* is an explicit claim of a current role. A blank end date may mean the person forgot to fill it in. Pick a convention, store which case occurred, and do not silently treat blanks as current.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Precision: majority vote, best-of-N and when they plateau
md: Repeated sampling scales **coverage** smoothly; selection without a reliable checker does not keep up. The useful question is never only how many samples, but how good is the verifier at the tail.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: One gradient step on a key-value loss is the delta rule
md: One step of online gradient descent on the regression loss is exactly the DeltaNet update with $\beta = \eta$. The TTT paper says so directly: DeltaNet is TTT-Linear with mini-batch size 1, minus the LayerNorm and residual. TTT is the framework; the delta rule is its simplest instance.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Sizing M, filling the depot, and the memory you pay
md: A per-CPU or per-thread cache is a deliberate trade of memory for scalability. Idle rounds look like a leak in heap profiles and RSS, and they multiply by the number of CPUs (or threads) and caches. Every production design pairs its caches with a sizing policy and a way to give memory back.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Forecasting is supervised learning where the future is off limits
md: A random train/test split on a time series leaks the future into training and makes every model look better than it will be in production. Hyndman and Athanasopoulos state the rule plainly: the training set may contain only observations that occurred before the test observations, so no future observations are used to construct the forecast.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Fused softmax: one row per program, reductions on chip
md: This design assumes a whole row fits in one block; the tutorial targets matrices whose rows fit in on-chip memory. For very long rows you would loop over chunks of the row inside the program and combine partial maxima and sums instead.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: One encoder or two: why Janus splits seeing from drawing
md: Shared vs separate encoders is a trade between simplicity and specialization. One encoder means one token type and one path, but semantic and reconstruction goals pull against each other. Two encoders let each path pick its best tool while the transformer still sees one sequence.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Booting on the hypervisor: virtual devices, boot time and memory
